tenures.capital_outlay_note: Sum of RBI capital-outlay actuals FY2014-15 to FY2018-19. Financial years approximate the tenure (it began June 2014, ended May 2019).
tenures.summary: The first government of the divided state: chose and founded Amaravati as the capital (PM laid the foundation, Oct 2015), signed the era's marquee industrial deals (Kia, Apollo Tyres, Hero, Isuzu at Sri City), ran welfare mainly through pensions (NTR Bharosa), SHG support (Pasupu Kumkuma) and a farm-loan waiver, and broke with its central ally in 2018 over Special Category Status. Its own final budget speech claims ₹24,618 Cr on pensions and ₹8,604 Cr to 86 lakh SHG women.

timeline.text: Andhra Pradesh begins as a divided state (AP Reorganisation Act 'appointed day'); Hyderabad becomes shared capital for 10 years.
N. Chandrababu Naidu sworn in as first Chief Minister of the divided state.
Prime Minister lays the foundation stone of the new capital Amaravati at Uddandarayunipalem.
Kia Motors signs its MoU for the ~USD 1.1 billion car plant at Anantapur — the tenure's biggest industrial win.
TDP exits the NDA over the Special Category Status dispute and moves a no-confidence motion against the central government.
Final (vote-on-account) budget presents the government's own tally of its welfare record — pensions ₹24,618 Cr, Pasupu Kumkuma ₹8,604 Cr, 71 lakh scholarships ₹12,833 Cr.
Election result: YSRCP 151 of 175 seats; TDP 23. The tenure ends.

tenures.capital_outlay_note: Sum of RBI capital-outlay figures FY2019-20 to FY2023-24 (FY2023-24 from RBI St.4 Accounts). Financial years approximate the tenure.
tenures.summary: A welfare-first government: converted most schemes to Direct Benefit Transfer under 'Navasakam' and, in its own final budget speech, claimed ₹2.53 lakh crore sent by DBT plus ₹1.68 lakh crore non-DBT — ₹4.21 lakh crore in all. It halted Amaravati works (the World Bank project lapsed after the Centre withdrew its financing request), pursued and then withdrew a three-capitals law, created 13 new districts, and saw capital outlay fall to its lowest-ever year (₹7,244 Cr, FY2022-23, per CAG) while social-sector spending rose sharply.

timeline.text: Y.S. Jagan Mohan Reddy sworn in as Chief Minister after winning 151 of 175 seats.
World Bank confirms the proposed USD 300M Amaravati project is dropped — 'On July 15 the Government of India withdrew its request… for financing.'
Three-capitals plan announced in the Assembly (executive Visakhapatnam, legislative Amaravati, judicial Kurnool); Amaravati farmers' protests begin.
Decentralisation and CRDA-repeal bills receive the Governor's assent.
Government withdraws the three-capitals legislation, saying an improved bill would follow.
13 new districts created — Andhra Pradesh now has 26 districts.
Former CM Chandrababu Naidu arrested by AP CID in the skill-development-corporation case; sent to 14-day judicial custody.

Final (vote-on-account) budget states the government's own welfare tally: '₹2.53 lakh crore was spent through DBT between 2019-20 to 2023-24… ₹4.21 lakh crore has thus been transferred to the hands of the people.'
Election result: NDA 164 of 175 seats; YSRCP 11. The tenure ends.

tenures.capital_outlay_note: Only estimates exist so far: ₹24,072.5 Cr (FY2024-25 revised estimate) and ₹40,635.7 Cr budgeted for FY2025-26 — audited actuals for this tenure are not yet published, so no total is shown.
tenures.summary: The current government: restarted Amaravati (PM laid foundations of ₹58,000+ Cr of capital works, May 2025), secured a Union-budget commitment of ₹15,000 Cr capital support and Polavaram completion (revised cost ₹30,436.95 Cr approved Aug 2024), rolled out the 'Super Six' welfare set (pension raise to ₹4,000, Thalliki Vandanam, Deepam-2, Annadata Sukhibhava, free bus travel for women), and pitched heavily for investment (Google's $15 bn Visakhapatnam AI hub, CII Partnership Summit MoU claims of ₹11+ lakh crore — summit figures are announcements, not ground-broken investment). Budgeted capital outlay for FY2025-26 (₹40,636 Cr) is the highest ever proposed — a budget estimate, not yet spent.

timeline.text: N. Chandrababu Naidu sworn in as Chief Minister for the fourth time after the NDA won 164 of 175 seats.
Enhanced pensions (₹4,000/month standard; up to ₹10,000 for severe illness) disbursed from the first month.
Union Budget commits: '₹15,000 crore will be arranged' for the capital 'with additional amounts in future years', and 'financing and early completion of the Polavaram Irrigation Project'.
Union Cabinet approves Polavaram's revised cost of ₹30,436.95 crore, with a balance central grant of ₹12,157.53 crore.
Deepam-2 launched — three free LPG cylinders per year for eligible women.
PM lays foundations/inaugurates ₹58,000+ crore of Amaravati capital works — the capital's restart.
Thalliki Vandanam rolled out: ₹15,000 per school-going child paid to mothers — 67.27 lakh students in year one.
Stree Shakti launched — free APSRTC bus travel for women; nearly 40 crore women's journeys by Jan 2026 (government claim).
Google announces its first AI hub in India at Visakhapatnam with a $15 billion investment.

glossary.capital: Capital outlay is money that BUILDS something that lasts — school buildings, hospitals, roads, irrigation canals. It is different from running costs (salaries, pensions) and from welfare transfers. If the government were a family, this is the money spent building the house, not running it.
glossary.sector: This shows how much of every ₹100 the government spends goes to education and to health. A falling share does not always mean less money (the total budget grows) — it means the sector got a smaller slice of the pie.
glossary.committed: Salaries, pensions and interest must be paid before anything else — CAG calls this 'committed expenditure'. When ₹65 of every ₹100 of income is committed, only ₹35 remains for everything else: schemes, repairs, and building new things.
glossary.schemes: పథకాలు (schemes) are direct help to people — pensions, cash support, fee reimbursement. The amounts here are each government's OWN claims from its budget speeches. CAG does not separately audit most scheme totals, so treat them as claims, clearly labeled.
glossary.manifesto: A manifesto is the promise-list a party publishes before an election. We quote the promises as recorded and place them next to what official documents show was done — we do not give verdicts; you compare.
glossary.tenure: Governments serve five-year terms. Financial years end on 31 March but governments change in May–June, so per-tenure totals use the nearest financial years and say so. A project or payment can also span two governments — the timeline shows dates precisely so you can judge.
glossary.verify: How do we know money was really spent? Every figure has a stage. 'Budget estimate' = a promise. 'Revised estimate' = a mid-year correction. 'Actuals' = the money that actually moved — checked and certified by the CAG, India's constitutional auditor, and compiled by the RBI. Solid bars on our charts are those audited actuals. We never take spending figures from news articles.
glossary.rankings: These scores are published by the central government's own institutions (NITI Aayog, DPIIT, DARPG) — not by us and not by any party. Note what each measures: fiscal health and business reforms grade the state government; SDG and innovation indices grade conditions in the state, which many things beyond one government shape.
glossary.economy: Per-capita income is the state's total income divided by its population — the average per person, at current prices (so part of every rise is inflation). Revenue receipts are the government's own yearly income: its taxes plus its share from the Centre. Neither is one government's 'achievement' alone — but the trend under each tenure is a fact you can see.
glossary.awards_g: These are recognitions given by CENTRAL ministries — not by us and not by the state. An award to a city (like Visakhapatnam's cleanliness awards) credits that city's municipal body and its workers as much as any state government. Every entry links to the official record.
glossary.leaderboards: These are the central government's own statistical tables — published by the Reserve Bank of India from National Statistical Office data, the same numbers the Centre itself works with. Every state, every year, in one table. We rank each year's column exactly as published and mark where Andhra Pradesh stands. Nothing is adjusted except one unit change: the GSDP table is printed in ₹ lakh and we show ₹ crore. A dash means the Centre has not published that figure — we never fill a gap ourselves.

rankings.intro: The central government's own institutions score every state, edition by edition. These are the closest thing to an official 'leaderboard'. metrics.label: Per-person income (per-capita NSDP)
metrics.explain: Take everything a state's economy produced in a year (minus wear-and-tear of machines and buildings), divide by its population — that is per-capita NSDP. It is the fairest single number for comparing big and small states, because Uttar Pradesh producing more than Sikkim in total says nothing about how the average person is doing. 'Current prices' means the rupee figures of that year itself, not adjusted for inflation — so compare states within a year freely, but remember that growth across years includes price rises.

metrics.label: State GDP (GSDP)
metrics.explain: GSDP is the value of everything produced inside the state in a year — the state's total economic size. Bigger states naturally have bigger GSDP, so use this to see scale, and use per-person income to see how the average citizen fares. 'Current prices' means no inflation adjustment.

metrics.explain: A state's outstanding liabilities measured against the size of its economy — like comparing a family's loans to its yearly income. ₹1 lakh crore of debt is heavy for a small economy and light for a huge one, so this ratio is how debt burdens are honestly compared across states. Lower is safer; the 15th Finance Commission's glide path pointed states toward roughly the low 30s or below.

head_to_head.intro: Two full governments and one in progress. On the left of each card is what that government said — its manifesto promises and its own claimed scheme spending. On the right is what the record shows — audited spending, the projects and MoUs on file, and how the economy and the debt moved. We put both side by side and let you judge; we never score a government.
fair_comparison: Tenure lengths differ. TDP 2014–19 and YSRCP 2019–24 each ran five financial years; the present government has two on record so far, and its later years are estimates, not audited actuals. Totals are shown with a per-year figure beside them for that reason.

The financial year ending March 2021 falls inside the YSRCP tenure and covers the COVID-19 lockdown period — revenue collapsed and spending patterns broke across every Indian state that year. A dip there is not, by itself, a verdict on a government; nor is it an excuse for every later year. We flag the year and leave the reading to you.
'Claimed' figures are each government's own numbers from its budget speeches and releases. They have not been audited against the CAG's accounts and are never mixed into the audited series.
An MoU shown as operational had to have time to get there — the oldest commitments have had a decade, the newest a year. Read the operational share with that in mind.

Projects 'completed in tenure' counts records whose completion date falls inside that tenure, whoever started them. Where a project spans a handover, its own page shows the split and says plainly where the record cannot divide it.
head_to_head.covid_note: COVID-19 year — nationwide lockdown from late March 2020; the financial year ending March 2021 is not comparable to a normal year for any state.

tenure_stories._note: Narrative sections for each government. Every sentence that carries a figure names the document it came from, and every document is in the sources list. Where an official figure does not exist, the text says so instead of estimating.
tenure_stories.intro: A tenure is more than a column of numbers. These are the events the official record documents for each government, in plain words, with the document behind every figure. We describe what happened; we do not grade it.

tdp1.headline: A state starting over, and a bill the two sides never agreed on

paragraphs.text: Andhra Pradesh began this term without its capital, without Hyderabad's revenues, and in deficit. A study commissioned by the Fifteenth Finance Commission put the state's 2014-15 revenue deficit at ₹13,775.76 crore even after an ad hoc central grant of ₹2,303 crore; without that grant the gap was ₹16,078.76 crore.

What the state claimed and what the Centre accepted never met. Against Andhra Pradesh's resource-gap claim, the Centre approved ₹4,117.89 crore on standardised expenditure calculations and released ₹3,979.50 crore, rejecting claims of roughly ₹11,960.87 crore — including the farm loan waiver and DISCOM assistance. That disagreement, not any single scheme, shaped the term's finances.

Money did arrive. The Ministry of Finance recorded ₹22,113 crore payable to Andhra Pradesh as a revenue deficit grant over five years, and by September 2016 ₹2,500 crore had been disbursed for the new capital with ₹1,000 crore pending, plus ₹1,050 crore of the backward-areas package. Tax devolution jumped ₹7,787 crore in 2015-16 alone, a rise of 55 per cent.

Under Section 94(3) of the AP Reorganisation Act, the Home Ministry told the Rajya Sabha that ₹1,500 crore had gone to capital city infrastructure and ₹1,000 crore as one-time special assistance for Vijayawada and Guntur.

Polavaram, declared a national project, was approved at ₹16,010.45 crore at 2010-11 prices, with the Centre committed to fund the whole remaining irrigation cost from April 2014. Central assistance released up to 2017-18 came to ₹4,906.99 crore, and releases in the term's later years were ₹2,514.70 crore (2016-17), ₹2,000 crore (2017-18) and ₹1,400 crore (2018-19).

The state's own earning never caught up with the plan. The 14th Finance Commission projected own tax revenue at 7.98 per cent of GSDP for 2015-16; the state reached 6.65 per cent, and the shortfall persisted. This is the thread that runs through all three governments.

tdp1.not_on_record: No CAG, PIB or state document we could open states what the term spent in total on building Amaravati, or totals actual releases against the 'special assistance in lieu of special category status' commitment. We leave both blank rather than estimate.

ysrcp.headline: Two years the pandemic took, and what the record shows about them

paragraphs.text: India's lockdown began on 24 March 2020 and the Home Ministry extended it to 31 May 2020 — the opening weeks of the financial year ending March 2021. Every state's books broke that year, and Andhra Pradesh's broke in a way the auditor described precisely.

The state's income collapsed against its own plan. CAG recorded revenue receipts of ₹1,17,136 crore in 2020-21 — just 72.32 per cent of the ₹1,61,958 crore budgeted. Own tax revenue actually fell, from ₹57,601 crore to ₹57,409 crore, and the share of Union taxes dropped 13.39 per cent to ₹24,460 crore. CAG's own words: the pandemic 'resulted in the economic slowdown in the country that led to the decrease in receipts under tax and non-tax revenue'.

One line went up instead of down: grants-in-aid rose 45.69 per cent to ₹31,872 crore. That is the Centre's hand in the year — and the economy behind the taxes had stalled, with GSDP growth falling to 1.58 per cent from 11.53 per cent.

The Centre also changed the rules on borrowing. For 2020-21 states were allowed an extra 2 per cent of GSDP, lifting the ceiling from 3 to 5 per cent: half a per cent unconditional, one per cent tied to four reforms, and the last half per cent on completing at least three of them. Andhra Pradesh was among the first five states cleared, taking ₹2,525 crore for One Nation One Ration Card, and became the second state to finish power-sector reform for a further ₹1,515 crore. Having completed all four, it received permission for ₹9,190 crore.

GST compensation came as loans, not grants. Under the special window the state received ₹1,936.53 crore as a back-to-back loan by 3 February 2021, and ₹905.59 crore in the final tranche of the 2021-22 window.

The bill for that year was large. The revenue deficit reached ₹35,541 crore (3.60 per cent of GSDP) and the fiscal deficit ₹55,168 crore (5.59 per cent), breaching the state's own 5 per cent FRBM target, while outstanding liabilities hit ₹3,48,246 crore — 35.30 per cent of GSDP, over the 35 per cent ceiling.

On COVID itself, the audited figure is modest: the state received ₹580.25 crore from central authorities for pandemic relief and spent ₹337.25 crore on COVID measures across the health sector in 2020-21. No official breakdown of vaccination, oxygen or hospital spending beyond that was found.

The recovery in the next year was real and fast. Revenue receipts rose 28.53 per cent to ₹1,50,552 crore, own tax revenue 23.64 per cent to ₹70,979 crore, and the revenue deficit fell 75.77 per cent to ₹8,611 crore while the fiscal deficit more than halved to ₹25,013 crore. That is the number a fair reading has to hold beside the 2020-21 collapse.

The recovery came with a caveat the auditor put in writing. Reported liabilities for 2021-22 were ₹3,72,503 crore, or 31.00 per cent of GSDP and inside the target — but adding ₹1,18,394 crore of off-budget borrowing took the real ratio to 40.85 per cent. The headline met the rule; the full picture did not.
Polavaram continued through the term: in July 2023 the Centre approved a further ₹10,911.15 crore for work to a water level of 41.15 metres, plus ₹2,000 crore for repair of damages.

Looking back across the term, NITI Aayog's assessment was that Andhra Pradesh collects less than a median state — 13.4 per cent of GSDP in 2022-23 against 19.9 per cent — and ran a revenue deficit of 2.2 per cent where a median state ran a surplus.

ysrcp.not_on_record: The total additional borrowing Andhra Pradesh actually availed under the full 2 per cent relaxation is not stated state-wise in any release we could open, and no AP-specific share of the free-foodgrain programme was published. We show only what is documented.

tdp2.headline: A young term, with the Centre's commitments written into a budget speech

paragraphs.text: The Union Budget of July 2024 addressed the state directly. On the capital: 'Recognizing the state's need for a capital, we will facilitate special financial support through multilateral development agencies. In the current financial year ₹15,000 crore will be arranged, with additional amounts in future years.' On irrigation, the government declared itself 'fully committed to financing and early completion of the Polavaram Irrigation Project, which is the lifeline for Andhra Pradesh and its farmers.'

The same speech promised infrastructure funding for the Kopparthy node on the Visakhapatnam-Chennai Industrial Corridor and the Orvakal node on the Hyderabad-Bengaluru corridor, along with grants for Rayalaseema, Prakasam and North Coastal Andhra as set out in the Reorganisation Act. The Cabinet then approved 12 industrial nodes nationally, Orvakal and Kopparthy among them, though no node-wise investment figure was published.

The multilateral money arrived as approvals in December 2024: $800 million from the World Bank and $788.8 million from the Asian Development Bank for the Amaravati Integrated Urban Development Program, part of a $1.78 billion first phase covering a 320-km arterial road grid, 1,280 km of neighbourhood roads, and water, wastewater and drainage systems.

The state's own 2025-26 budget put total expenditure at ₹2,97,929 crore against receipts excluding borrowings of ₹2,18,002 crore, with a revenue deficit of ₹33,186 crore (1.8 per cent of GSDP), a fiscal deficit of ₹79,927 crore (4.4 per cent) and debt at 35 per cent of GSDP. The largest allocations were ₹19,899 crore for NTR Bharosa pensions, ₹20,492 crore for education teaching grants, ₹11,883 crore for agricultural power subsidy, ₹6,705 crore for Polavaram, ₹6,300 crore for Annadata Sukhibhava and ₹6,000 crore for Amaravati.

tdp2.not_on_record: No official figure exists yet for how much of the ₹15,000 crore capital support announced in the Union Budget has actually been disbursed. The speech states it 'will be arranged'; the World Bank and ADB approvals confirm the mechanism, not a rupee total. Most of this term's spending figures are still estimates, not audited actuals.
